chunks.section: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the LoRA Fine-Tuning Landscape with Implications for Data Selection
chunks.text: Bowen Zhang Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong Changrui Fang Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong Xinsong Ma Affiliation: City University of Hong Kong Jiaye Teng Affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Ziye Ma † † thanks: Corresponding author. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. Our central insight is that the appropriate adapter rank should depend on the quality of the data-induced optimization geometry, rather than on the model alone. To formalize this connection, we introduce LoRA-RIP, a data-dependent restricted-isometry metric that characterizes the conditioning of the cross-entropy (CE) objective along LoRA-relevant low-rank directions. We prove that sufficient rank over-parameterization, with the required rank explicitly determined by the LoRA-RIP constant, eliminates spurious local minima, thereby extending existing RIP-based guarantees beyond the classical 1 / 3 1/3 regime. This characterization further enables principled data selection under a fixed rank budget. Experiments across language and vision tasks support these theoretical predictions, showing that rank and data quality are two coupled resources that should be jointly considered for more efficient and reliable LoRA fine-tuning.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a standard parameter-efficient method for fine-tuning large models ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Given a pretrained weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ n 1 × n 2 W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} , LoRA freezes W 0 W_{0} and learns an additive low-rank update W = W 0 + γ ​ M W=W_{0}+\gamma M , where M = U ​ V ⊤ M=UV^{\top} , U ∈ ℝ n 1 × r U\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times r} , V ∈ ℝ n 2 × r V\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}\times r} , and γ \gamma is a scaling factor. With r ≪ min ⁡ ( n 1 , n 2 ) r\ll\min(n_{1},n_{2}) , this factorization reduces the trainable parameter count for the adapted matrix from n 1 ​ n 2 n_{1}n_{2} to r ⁡ ( n 1 + n 2 ) r(n_{1}+n_{2}) , lowering optimizer-state and memory requirements while often maintaining strong downstream performance. Realizing these efficiency gains, however, requires an appropriate choice of the adapter rank. Although larger ranks offer greater expressivity ( Zeng and Lee, 2024 ) , their practical value cannot be judged from representational capacity alone. In linearized fine-tuning experiments, Jang et al. (2024) observe that lower ranks converge more slowly even when they ultimately reach the same loss. Conversely, increasing rank need not improve downstream performance. For example, Albert et al. (2024) report that, when fine-tuning Phi3 on 15,000 examples, increasing the LoRA rank from 16 16 to 32 32 reduces the reported mean accuracy across eight commonsense reasoning tasks from 81.8 % 81.8\% to 80.3 % 80.3\% . These observations illustrate the cost of an unsuitable rank choice: an overly restrictive rank can slow optimization, whereas an unnecessarily large rank can consume additional resources without corresponding performance gains. This leaves a complementary question: how should adapter rank be chosen to support effective fine-tuning without unnecessary parameter overhead?

This question naturally leads us to nonconvex low-rank optimization: LoRA learns a factorized update, with the adapter rank r r controlling its degree of parameterization ( Burer and Monteiro, 2003 ) . A long line of work has characterized the landscapes of factorized problems and established conditions excluding spurious local minima ( Bhojanapalli et al., 2016 ; Ge et al., 2017 ; Zhu et al., 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) . In classical matrix sensing, the restricted isometry property (RIP) is a key metric that characterizes the optimization landscape, and it measures how uniformly the sensing data capture low-rank structure, making its constant a natural indicator of the underlying data geometry ( Recht et al., 2010 ) . More recent advances show that rank over-parameterization can improve the landscape by eliminating spurious local minima under weaker RIP conditions ( Zhang, 2025a ; Zhang, 2025b ) , directly connecting search rank with data-induced geometry. Classical sensing, however, assumes a fixed ℓ 2 \ell_{2} objective in matrix space, whereas LoRA settings have cross-entropy loss coupling with the base model structure. Its geometry therefore varies with the model’s responses to the data and the adapter update, making the extension of classical rank–RIP analysis nontrivial. Specifically for the LoRA fine-tuning landscape, Jang et al. (2024) establish no-spurious-minima guarantees in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime, while Liu et al. (2025) further relate adapter rank to local optimization geometry under ℓ 2 \ell_{2} loss. These results demonstrate the relevance of landscape theory, but their reliance on local linearization or squared-loss settings limits the guidance they provide for nonlinear cross-entropy fine-tuning. Their global-optimality guarantee in the analyzed region corresponds to a RIP constant below 1 / 3 1/3 , while larger values allow a “fails-loudly” alternative. However, their analysis leaves two important aspects insufficiently characterized: the CE-specific structure of the RIP constant in LoRA, and how the adapter rank r r shapes the optimization landscape beyond the small-RIP regime. Since RIP is strongly determined by the geometry of the fine-tuning data, these two questions are closely connected: understanding LoRA optimization requires relating data-induced RIP to the role of rank in shaping the landscape. Clarifying this relationship is therefore a key step toward a more principled theory of rank choice in LoRA fine-tuning.

We introduce a new data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant, denoted by δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} . Under the stated assumptions, we establish an explicit relation between r / r ⋆ r/r_{\star} and δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} that guarantees a landscape free of spurious local minima, where r ⋆ r_{\star} refers to the rank of the global solution. This implies that any algorithm that can converge to a second-order stationary point (SOSP) 1 1 1 For definition of SOSP please see Appendix B.1 in polynomial time can reach the global solution reliably. More importantly, our results hold in the regime where δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} exceeds 1 / 3 1/3 , and show that larger ranks permit larger LoRA-RIP values in the guarantee. Under common curvature bounds covering the ranks considered, this characterization yields a sufficient constant-factor rank requirement relative to r ⋆ r_{\star} , with the factor determined by the LoRA-RIP bound. Once this requirement is met, further rank is unnecessary for the same guarantee within that range. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has become a central parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, and numerous variants have been built on its structure, including quantized adapters ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) , adaptive rank allocation ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and modified factor updates ( Hayou et al., 2024 ) . Other work studies geometric updates and stabilization mechanisms ( Zhang and Pilanci, 2024 ; Yen et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Recent theory has studied LoRA from complementary angles. Expressivity results characterize what a given adapter rank can represent ( Zeng and Lee, 2024 ) . From the view of optimization, NTK-regime analysis gives benign landscape guarantees for a linearized fine-tuning model ( Jang et al., 2024 ) . Other works analyze nonlinear LoRA landscapes or gradient-flow dynamics under structural assumptions ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) .

Low-rank matrix optimization provides a geometric foundation for understanding factorized objectives. A rank-constrained variable is often written as X = U ​ V ⊤ X=UV^{\top} by Burer-Monteiro factorization ( Burer and Monteiro, 2003 ) , which replaces the rank constraint by a nonconvex optimization problem over the factors. For matrix recovery and related objectives, restricted curvature or RIP-type conditions can imply benign landscape properties, such as the absence of spurious local minima or strict-saddle geometry ( Ge et al., 2017 ; Zhu et al., 2018 ) . Similar geometric analyses have also been developed for more general low-rank objectives ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) . A more recent direction studies rank over-parameterization: when the search rank exceeds the target rank r ⋆ r_{\star} , the required amount of over-parameterization can be expressed through RIP quantities ( Zhang, 2025a ; Zhang, 2025b ) .

As innovations in model architecture hit a plateau, the strategic selection of training data becomes increasingly crucial. Existing work includes Shapley-based data valuation ( Ghorbani and Zou, 2019 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , gradient-based data attribution and selection ( Pruthi et al., 2020 ; Xia et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) and similarity-based data filtering ( Sachdeva et al., 2026 ; Das et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, recent theoretical work explores the statistical properties ( Allouah et al., 2026 ; Rezaei et al., 2026 ) . Complementary work studies training geometry through Hessian spectra and cross-entropy dynamics ( Ghorbani et al., 2019 ; Garrod et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we connect data composition to LoRA rank requirements through the optimization geometry of the cross-entropy objective.

chunks.section: 5.2 Data Selection Criteria Based on LoRA-RIP
chunks.text: The certificate above turns data selection into the problem of improving the data-side LoRA-RIP certificate, which leads to several selection rules we discuss below:
We run some numerical experiments to validate our qualitative view on data selection and landscape results. Relevant code can be found in the supplementary materials.

We consider one language task and one vision task. For NLP, we fine-tune MPNet-base ( Song et al., 2020 ) on MNLI ( Williams et al., 2018 ) , a natural-language inference task in GLUE ( Wang et al., 2018 ) . For vision, we fine-tune a ViT-B/16 model ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2020 ) on CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky and Hinton, 2009 ) . In each run, we apply LoRA to the query projection in layer/block 10. Each experiment controls all other training choices except for the single factor being tested. Full protocols and complete results for the main-text experiments are provided in Appendix D . We further offer curvature diagnostics, multi-seed evaluations, and robustness studies across datasets and adaptation settings in Appendix E .

The rank sweep isolates the role of the search rank while keeping the data distribution fixed. Because our theory concerns the cross-entropy objective rather than classification accuracy alone, we report validation CE as the primary metric. Figure 1 shows an extended sweep over r ∈ { 1 , 4 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 , 512 } r\in\{1,4,16,32,64,128,256,512\} . The second experiment tests the data-selection prediction from Section 5.2 on MNLI. We keep the subset size and label counts fixed, and change only how examples are distributed across gradient groups. These groups are built from a random-projected margin-Jacobian feature at the adapted matrix, so they act as a practical proxy for which LoRA directions the data cover; see Appendix C.5 . We compare balanced coverage with light and heavy long-tail coverage. Figure 2 shows that balanced coverage performs best overall. Long-tail sampling hurts validation accuracy, especially under heavy long-tail sampling and at smaller ranks. This matches the LoRA-RIP view: if too many examples come from the same gradient groups, the data repeatedly cover the same directions while leaving other useful directions weakly observed. In the notation of Section 5.2 , this worsens the balance between the coverage floor c ν , k c_{\nu,k} and ceiling C ν , k C_{\nu,k} . The gap shrinks as rank increases. By r = 64 r=64 , balanced and light long-tail sampling have similar validation accuracy, although balanced sampling still gives better test accuracy. The remaining gains at larger ranks underscore the complementary roles of adapter rank and data composition, consistent also with our landscape results. Additional multi-seed robustness and curvature diagnostics are provided in Appendices E.4 , E.5 , and E.6 . Figure 2: Validation-accuracy trajectories for the MNLI gradient-coverage intervention.

The third experiment evaluates confidence-aware selection while keeping subset size, label counts, and gradient-group quotas fixed. Within each group, we select easy, middle, or near-boundary examples using the shared reference model; Appendix D.5 describes the construction. Figure 3 shows that both Middle and Boundary outperform Easy in the controlled MNLI comparison. The multi-seed results in Appendix E.7 also show higher mean validation accuracy for both less-saturated bands than for Easy at every tested rank, while their relative ordering varies with rank. These performance results are qualitatively consistent with the limited softmax-side curvature leverage of highly saturated examples in Section 5.2 . The practical implication is to use confidence alongside directional coverage and avoid concentrating the data budget on highly saturated examples. Figure 3: Validation-accuracy trajectories for the MNLI saturation-band intervention.

We studied how adapter rank and fine-tuning data jointly shape LoRA’s optimization landscape under cross-entropy loss. Under the stated assumptions, rank over-parameterization relative to the target rank rules out spurious local minima, with the required factor explicitly determined by our data-dependent LoRA-RIP constant δ k LoRA \delta_{k}^{\mathrm{LoRA}} . The guarantee also covers LoRA-RIP values above 1 / 3 1/3 , quantifying how additional rank can compensate for less favorable geometry to achieve a benign landscape. Our framework further motivates data selection under a fixed rank budget, yielding principles based on latent-space coverage and pre-tuning softmax saturation. Experiments support these insights into the interplay between rank and data composition. However, most of the bounds presented in this work are sufficient, and an important future direction is to shorten their gap with necessary ones.

chunks.section: Appendix E Landscape Diagnostics and Robustness Evaluations
chunks.text: This section examines the optimization geometry and stability of LoRA fine-tuning through rank/checkpoint curvature, ambient matrix-space references, and multi-seed training. We also study the effects of data composition at a common reference point and along training trajectories, evaluate coverage across datasets, backbones, and adapter locations, and examine confidence-band selection on MNLI. The rank-sweep and MNLI data-intervention protocols are described in Appendix D . Together, these evaluations connect rank-dependent optimization gains to data-induced geometry and the practical effectiveness of landscape-guided selection.

Unless stated otherwise, the diagnostics use MPNet-base on MNLI, a frozen linear-probe head, a frozen backbone, and a LoRA update on the layer-10 query projection. Every coverage condition contains 17,526 17{,}526 unique training examples with label counts 5,847 / 5,788 / 5,891 5{,}847/5{,}788/5{,}891 . The rank/checkpoint diagnostic uses ranks 4 , 64 , 128 , 256 4,64,128,256 , optimization seeds 0 , 1 , 2 0,1,2 , and start, middle, and final checkpoints (epochs 0 , 5 , 10 0,5,10 ). It evaluates projected logit-Jacobian and CE-Hessian actions in the same 24 24 -dimensional basis. Our theoretical analysis focuses on single-matrix LoRA fine-tuning with cross-entropy loss under low-rank target and LoRA-RIP assumptions. The resulting rank bounds are sufficient rather than necessary, leaving room for tighter characterizations of the relationship between adapter rank and data-induced geometry. Our empirical evaluation examines this relationship through controlled classification experiments across datasets and backbones. Extending the theory to joint multi-layer adaptation and evaluating the data-selection principles in larger-scale generative fine-tuning are natural directions for future work.
